title: 1.3 Small Group · Group 2
contentObjective: I can represent a real-world situation with a tape diagram or table and use decimal operations to solve it, explain what each part stands for, and build one for a situation I have not seen before.
languageObjective: I can justify my answer to a skeptic and connect it to a second strategy or representation.

noticeAndWonder.context: An aerial tramway car glides on a cable high above a valley, carrying passengers from the station below toward the mountain top.
noticeStarters: I notice the cable car route ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder how long one trip ___ .
I wonder how many trips are needed ___ .

vocabulary.definition: A picture, diagram, table, or equation that shows the mathematics in a situation.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un dibujo, diagrama, tabla o ecuación que muestra las matemáticas de una situación.
vocabulary.example: A tape diagram representing 4,000 passengers split into tram rides.
vocabulary.visual: The same 12 shown three ways: a tape diagram, a table, and 3 × 4.
vocabulary.cloze: A drawing, table, or equation that shows the math in a situation is a ___.

examples.text: A table pairing rides with minutes
examples.why: It shows the mathematics of the situation in an organized form.

examples.text: A drawing of the tram because it looks nice
examples.why: A picture that carries no quantities shows no mathematics.

vocabulary.definition: A rectangle cut into equal parts that helps you visualize how a total breaks apart.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un rectángulo dividido en partes iguales que te ayuda a visualizar cómo se separa un total.
vocabulary.example: A bar for 4,000 passengers cut into equal groups of 80.
vocabulary.visual: One bar of 4,000 passengers cut into equal groups of 80.
vocabulary.cloze: A rectangle cut into equal parts that shows how a total breaks apart is a ___ ___.

examples.text: A bar split into 5 equal parts to share $53.50
examples.why: The bar is the total and the parts are equal shares.

examples.text: A bar with parts of different sizes and no labels
examples.why: Without equal, labelled parts it does not model the total.

vocabulary.definition: Anything you choose to help you see relationships and solve a problem — a table, a diagram, a graph.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cualquier cosa que eliges para ver relaciones y resolver un problema: una tabla, un diagrama, una gráfica.
vocabulary.example: A table of values relating minutes to round trips.
vocabulary.visual: A table, a number line, or a tape diagram — whichever shows the relationship.
vocabulary.cloze: Anything you choose to help you see relationships and solve is a ___.

examples.text: Choosing a table because you need to see every step
examples.why: You picked it on purpose to reveal the mathematics.

examples.text: A calculator used before you know what to compute
examples.why: A tool helps you think; it cannot decide what the problem asks.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers that go together, like a time and a number of trips, that you can plot as a point.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos números que van juntos, como un tiempo y un número de viajes, que puedes graficar como un punto.
vocabulary.visual: (4, 60): 4 hours costs $60 — the hours always come first.
vocabulary.cloze: Two numbers that go together and can be plotted as a point are an ___ ___.

examples.why: The order is reversed, so the point lands somewhere else.

vocabulary.definition: A complete journey from the start, to the destination, and back to the start.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un recorrido completo desde el inicio hasta el destino y de regreso al inicio.
vocabulary.example: The tram's 5-mile round trip from valley to mountain top and back takes 35 minutes.
vocabulary.visual: 5 miles out plus 5 miles back = 10 miles in all.
vocabulary.cloze: A journey out to a place and all the way back is a ___ ___.

examples.text: The tram car going up the mountain and back down
examples.why: It ends where it started, so both legs count.

examples.text: Riding the tram to the top and staying there
examples.why: Only half the journey has happened.

launch.narrative: This is your challenge small group for Lesson 1.3. You can already get the answer — so in here the answer is the starting point. We ask when the method holds, when it breaks, and how you would convince someone who disagrees.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — Visualize the problem, then choose a tool
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. So we go up a level, not up a number: find what is always true, show it a second way, and be ready to defend it with a reason instead of an answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: When we do math, we visualize and represent problems, use tools to show relationships among quantities, and make strategic decisions about which tool fits the problem — and you can say why it is true, and where it would stop being true.

iDo.title: Watch me estimate the coins
lines: A pile of coins is too big to count one at a time. About how many coins are in the pile?
I do not count every coin — I find a small stack I CAN count, about 10 coins.
Then I estimate how many stacks like that are in the pile. I count about 15.
15 stacks of about 10 is 15 × 10 = 150, so my estimate is about 150 coins — reasoned, not random.
linesEs: Un montón de monedas es demasiado grande para contarlo una por una. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas monedas hay en el montón?
No cuento cada moneda — busco una pila pequeña que sí pueda contar, de unas 10 monedas.
Luego estimo cuántas pilas así hay en el montón. Cuento unas 15.
15 pilas de unas 10 son 15 × 10 = 150, así que mi estimación es de unas 150 monedas — razonada, no al azar.

weDo.title: Try it together — then prove it
lines: One tram ride takes 12.5 minutes, so 10 rides take 12.5 × 10 = 125 minutes and 50 rides take 12.5 × 50 = 625 minutes.
The tram needs 50 rides to move 4,000 passengers, and 625 minutes is 625 ÷ 60 hours — about 10.42 hours.
A tape diagram of 4,000 cut into equal rides shows WHY we divide, and the table shows how minutes grow with rides.
Now prove it: say why that move had to work at all — not just that it did.
Sentence frame — convince a skeptic: "My method works because ___ . It would stop working if ___ ."
linesEs: Un viaje del teleférico toma 12.5 minutos, así que 10 viajes toman 12.5 × 10 = 125 minutos y 50 viajes toman 12.5 × 50 = 625 minutos.
El teleférico necesita 50 viajes para mover a 4,000 pasajeros, y 625 minutos son 625 ÷ 60 horas — unas 10.42 horas.
Un diagrama de barras de 4,000 repartido en viajes iguales muestra por qué dividimos, y la tabla muestra cómo crecen los minutos con los viajes.
Ahora demuéstralo: di por qué ese paso tenía que funcionar — no solo que funcionó.
Marco de oración — convence a alguien que duda: «Mi método funciona porque ___ . Dejaría de funcionar si ___ .»

youDo.title: Now you try — and defend it
lines: Try the problems below on your own. Getting the answer is half the work — be ready to say why your method works, and where it would stop working.
Then pick one problem and show it a second way. If two different methods agree, that agreement is your proof.
linesEs: Intenta los problemas de abajo por tu cuenta. Obtener la respuesta es la mitad del trabajo — prepárate para decir por qué funciona tu método y dónde dejaría de funcionar.
Luego elige un problema y muéstralo de una segunda manera. Si dos métodos distintos coinciden, esa coincidencia es tu prueba.

conceptIntro.headingEs: Ve más allá — Visualiza el problema y luego elige una herramienta
conceptIntro.introEs: Esto ya lo sabes hacer. Así que subimos de nivel, no de número: halla lo que siempre es cierto, muéstralo de una segunda manera y prepárate para defenderlo con una razón en lugar de una respuesta.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Cuando hacemos matemáticas, visualizamos y representamos problemas, usamos herramientas para mostrar relaciones entre cantidades y decidimos con estrategia qué herramienta le queda al problema — y puedes decir por qué es cierto y dónde dejaría de serlo.

explore.label: Which operation fits the job? Sort the tram tasks.

cards.text: Find how many rides are needed for 4,000 passengers if each ride carries 80
Find the total minutes for 50 rides at 12.5 minutes each
Find how many 35-minute round trips fit in 600 minutes
Find the total miles a tram car travels in 17 round trips of 5 miles each
Split 2,000 passengers into equal rides of 80
Find how many passengers ride in 25 rides of 80 passengers each

explore.instructions: Go deeper: The book says we can use different operations for different parts of the problem. Sort each task by the operation that helps, then tell a partner how a tape diagram could show one of the division tasks. As you work, ask yourself WHY it works.

connect.scenario: It takes 35 minutes for one tram car to make the 5-mile round trip, from valley to mountain top and back down — including time for passengers to disembark and embark at each station. You want to know how many round trips a single tram car completes in 10 hours.
connect.promptQuestion: What tool can you use to represent the relationship between time and round trips, and how does it answer the question?
connect.prompt: Name the tool you would use to show the relationship — a ___ of values — then name the two quantities in the problem: ___ and ___ .

check.stem: The tram problem asks how many round trips fit in 10 hours. What is the FIRST thing you must find before you can read the answer off your table?
choices: How many minutes are in 10 hours, so the units match the table
How many miles the tram travels in total
How many passengers ride each trip
check.explanation: The table is built in minutes, but the question gives hours. Convert first: 10 hours = 600 minutes. Now you can find where 600 falls among the table's rows.

check.stem: Using the table (35→1, 175→5, 350→10, 525→15, 700→20 minutes→trips), why does the answer end up being 17 round trips, not 18?
choices: 17 trips take 595 minutes, which fits within 600, but an 18th trip would need 630 minutes, past the limit
18 trips is closer to 600 minutes, so it is the better estimate
A round trip can be counted as complete even if it is only partly finished
The table only lists rows up to 20, so 17 is the safe middle choice
check.explanation: Try 17 trips: 17 × 35 = 595 minutes. That is still inside the 600-minute limit. Try 18: 18 × 35 = 630 minutes, which goes past it. A round trip only counts once it is fully complete.

check.stem: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. Why is it risky to round this quotient down to 17 WITHOUT also checking the table?
choices: Rounding down happens to work here, but only the table confirms 17 × 35 stays under 600 while 18 × 35 does not
Rounding down never works for time problems
17.14 should round up to 18 because .14 rounds upward
The table and division always disagree with each other
check.explanation: 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.14. The .14 left over is an unfinished trip, not extra completed ones. Rounding alone does not prove that. Checking the table's real minute totals is what shows 17 is right.

connect.modelAnswer: The two quantities are the time and the number of round trips. I would build a table of values: 35 minutes for 1 trip, 175 for 5, 350 for 10, 525 for 15, 700 for 20. Ten hours is 600 minutes, which lands between 525 and 700 on my table. Since 17 trips take 595 minutes and an 18th trip would pass 600, a tram car completes 17 round trips in 10 hours. I could also plot the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane and read the answer there.

diagram.title: 2,000 Tram Passengers in Rides of 80
diagram.caption: Each group of 400 passengers takes 5 rides of 80; five groups reach 2,000 passengers and 25 rides, and 25 rides at 12.5 minutes each is 312.5 minutes.

onLevel.stem: The 50 rides take 625 minutes. About how many HOURS is that?
onLevel.explanation: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42, so it would take about 10.42 hours to transport 4,000 passengers.
choiceFeedback: 6.25 moves the decimal two places — that divides by 100, but an hour is 60 minutes.
62.5 divides by 10 — an hour is 60 minutes, not 10.
12.5 is the minutes for ONE ride, not the hours for all 50.
hints: How many minutes are in one hour?
Divide the total minutes by 60.
onLevel.stemEs: Los 50 viajes toman 625 minutos. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas HORAS son?
onLevel.explanationEs: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42, así que tomaría unas 10.42 horas transportar a 4,000 pasajeros.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos minutos tiene una hora?
Divide los minutos totales entre 60.

onLevel.stem: How does the answer change for 2,000 passengers? Each ride carries 80 passengers and takes 12.5 minutes. How many MINUTES are needed?
onLevel.explanation: 2,000 ÷ 80 = 25 rides, and 25 × 12.5 = 312.5 minutes — half the passengers, half the 625 minutes.
choiceFeedback: 31.25 shifts the decimal one place left — 25 × 12.5 is more than 25 × 10 = 250.
3,125 shifts the decimal one place right — check with estimation: 25 × 12.5 is close to 25 × 12 = 300.
300 uses 12 minutes per ride instead of 12.5 — the missing 0.5 costs 12.5 minutes across 25 rides.
hints: First find the rides: 2,000 ÷ 80.
That is 25 rides at 12.5 minutes each.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cómo cambia la respuesta para 2,000 pasajeros? Cada viaje lleva 80 pasajeros y toma 12.5 minutos. ¿Cuántos MINUTOS se necesitan?
onLevel.explanationEs: 2,000 ÷ 80 = 25 viajes, y 25 × 12.5 = 312.5 minutos — la mitad de los pasajeros, la mitad de los 625 minutos.
hintsEs: Halla primero los viajes: 2,000 ÷ 80.
Eso son 25 viajes de 12.5 minutos cada uno.

onLevel.stem: One round trip takes 35 minutes. Using the table (35 → 1, 350 → 10, 525 → 15, 700 → 20), how many round trips does a tram car complete in 10 hours?
onLevel.explanation: 10 hours is 600 minutes. 17 trips take 17 × 35 = 595 minutes, and an 18th trip would need 630 — past the 600. So the tram completes 17 round trips.
choiceFeedback: 20 trips is the 700-minute row — that is more time than the 600 minutes in 10 hours.
15 trips is the 525-minute row — that stops 75 minutes early, with time for two more trips.
18 rounds 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.1 UP, but the 18th trip is not finished within the 10 hours.
hints: Convert 10 hours to minutes first.
600 minutes falls between the 525 and 700 rows of the table.
600 ÷ 35 is about 17.1 — can a partial trip count as completed?
onLevel.stemEs: Un viaje de ida y vuelta toma 35 minutos. Usando la tabla (35 → 1, 350 → 10, 525 → 15, 700 → 20), ¿cuántos viajes de ida y vuelta completa una cabina del tranvía en 10 horas?
onLevel.explanationEs: 10 horas son 600 minutos. 17 viajes toman 17 × 35 = 595 minutos, y un viaje 18 necesitaría 630 — más de 600. Así que el tranvía completa 17 viajes de ida y vuelta.
hintsEs: Convierte primero las 10 horas a minutos.
600 minutos cae entre las filas de 525 y 700 de la tabla.
600 ÷ 35 es aproximadamente 17.1 — ¿puede contar como completado un viaje parcial?

onLevel.stem: The two tram problems both use the 35-minute or 12.5-minute ride times. How are the two problems the SAME, and how are they DIFFERENT?
onLevel.modelAnswer: They are the same because both relate time to a number of tram trips and both can use a table of values. They are different because the first starts from passengers and asks for total time, while the second starts from a total time (10 hours) and asks how many round trips fit inside it.
onLevel.stemEs: Los dos problemas del tranvía usan los tiempos de viaje de 35 minutos o de 12.5 minutos. ¿En qué se PARECEN los dos problemas y en qué se DIFERENCIAN?

extending.label: Each tram ride takes 12.5 minutes. Complete the table of total minutes.
extending.labelEs: Cada viaje del teleférico dura 12.5 minutos. Completa la tabla de minutos totales.
hints: Use the first row to build the others: 20 rides is double 10 rides.
50 rides is 5 × 10 rides — multiply your first answer by 5.
hintsEs: Usa la primera fila para construir las demás: 20 viajes es el doble de 10 viajes.
50 viajes es 5 × 10 viajes: multiplica tu primera respuesta por 5.
extending.explanation: 10 × 12.5 = 125 minutes. Doubling the rides doubles the time: 20 rides take 250 minutes. And 50 rides is five times 10 rides, so 5 × 125 = 625 minutes — the same 625 the lesson converts to about 10.4 hours.
extending.explanationEs: 10 × 12.5 = 125 minutos. Duplicar los viajes duplica el tiempo: 20 viajes toman 250 minutos. Y 50 viajes son cinco veces 10 viajes, así que 5 × 125 = 625 minutos, los mismos 625 que la lección convierte en unas 10.4 horas.

extending.label: Match each tram question to the operation that answers it.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada pregunta del teleférico con la operación que la responde.

pairs.termEs: Minutos de 40 viajes (12.5 min cada uno)

pairs.term: Rides needed for 400 passengers (80 per ride)
pairs.termEs: Viajes necesarios para 400 pasajeros (80 por viaje)

hints: Repeated groups → multiply. Splitting a total into groups → divide.
Check the units: minutes come from rides × minutes-per-ride; rides come from passengers ÷ passengers-per-ride.
hintsEs: Grupos repetidos → multiplica. Repartir un total en grupos → divide.
Revisa las unidades: los minutos salen de viajes × minutos por viaje; los viajes salen de pasajeros ÷ pasajeros por viaje.
extending.explanation: Choosing the operation is the modeling step: totals built from equal groups multiply (40 × 12.5 minutes; 30 × 80 passengers), while totals split into equal groups divide (400 ÷ 80 rides; 625 ÷ 60 to convert minutes to hours).
extending.explanationEs: Elegir la operación es el paso de modelar: los totales formados por grupos iguales se multiplican (40 × 12.5 minutos; 30 × 80 pasajeros), mientras que los totales repartidos en grupos iguales se dividen (400 ÷ 80 viajes; 625 ÷ 60 para convertir minutos a horas).

extending.stem: The round trip is 5 miles. How far does a tram car travel in 5 round trips?
extending.explanation: 5 round trips × 5 miles per trip = 25 miles.
choiceFeedback: 10 ADDS 5 + 5 instead of multiplying 5 trips by 5 miles.
50 is the distance for 10 round trips, not 5.
hints: Each trip covers the same 5 miles.
You need 5 equal groups of 5 miles.
extending.stemEs: El viaje de ida y vuelta es de 5 millas. ¿Qué distancia recorre una cabina del tranvía en 5 viajes de ida y vuelta?
extending.explanationEs: 5 viajes de ida y vuelta × 5 millas por viaje = 25 millas.
hintsEs: Cada viaje cubre las mismas 5 millas.
Necesitas 5 grupos iguales de 5 millas.

extending.stem: How does the answer change if the tram must transport 6,000 passengers? (Each ride carries 80 passengers and takes 12.5 minutes.) Show your steps.
extending.modelAnswer: 6,000 ÷ 80 = 75 rides. Then 75 × 12.5 = 937.5 minutes. Dividing by 60, that is 937.5 ÷ 60 = 15.625, so about 15.63 hours — half again as long as the 10.42 hours for 4,000 passengers, which makes sense because 6,000 is one and a half times 4,000.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cómo cambia la respuesta si el tranvía debe transportar a 6,000 pasajeros? (Cada viaje lleva 80 pasajeros y toma 12.5 minutos.) Muestra tus pasos.

extending.stem: Apply — What Time Is It? The new year starts at midnight on January 1st. What time will it be 2,022 minutes after midnight?
extending.explanation: 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 remainder 42, so 2,022 minutes is 33 hours 42 minutes. That is 24 hours (one full day) plus 9 hours 42 minutes — 9:42 a.m. on January 2.
choiceFeedback: That reads 2,022 minutes as 20 hours 22 minutes — but minutes must be DIVIDED by 60, not split by place value.
33 hours is more than one full day, so the clock has rolled past midnight into January 2.
After subtracting the 24-hour day, 9 hours 42 minutes past midnight is morning, not evening.
hints: Divide 2,022 by 60 to get hours and leftover minutes.
33 hours is one full day plus how many hours?
extending.stemEs: Aplica — ¿Qué hora es? El año nuevo empieza a la medianoche del 1 de enero. ¿Qué hora será 2,022 minutos después de la medianoche?
extending.explanationEs: 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 con residuo 42, así que 2,022 minutos son 33 horas y 42 minutos. Eso es 24 horas (un día completo) más 9 horas y 42 minutos — 9:42 a. m. del 2 de enero.
hintsEs: Divide 2,022 entre 60 para obtener horas y minutos sobrantes.
2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 con residuo 42.
33 horas son un día completo más ¿cuántas horas?

extending.stem: How many rides would the tram need for 10,000 passengers, at 80 passengers per ride?
extending.explanation: 10,000 ÷ 80 = 125 rides. Those rides would take 125 × 12.5 = 1,562.5 minutes.
choiceFeedback: 12.5 shifts the decimal one place too far — and 12.5 is also the minutes per ride, a different quantity.
250 divides 10,000 by 40 — that would only carry 40 passengers per ride.
hints: Split 10,000 into equal groups of 80.
Use the 4,000-passenger answer as an anchor: 4,000 needed 50 rides.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuántos viajes necesitaría el tranvía para 10,000 pasajeros, a 80 pasajeros por viaje?
hintsEs: Reparte 10,000 en grupos iguales de 80.
Usa la respuesta de 4,000 pasajeros como referencia: 4,000 necesitaron 50 viajes.

extending.stem: The lesson says we make strategic decisions about which tool to use. For the 10-hour round-trip question, would you choose a table of values, a coordinate plane, or an equation? Defend your choice.
extending.modelAnswer: I would choose the table of values, because I can extend the rows by 35 minutes at a time until I pass 600 minutes, and I can see that 600 lands between 525 and 700. A coordinate plane shows the same ordered pairs visually, and an equation like 35 × t ≤ 600 is fastest — any tool works if it shows the relationship between time and round trips, so the strategic part is picking the one I can read most clearly.
sentenceStems: Another tool that could work is ___ .
extending.stemEs: La lección dice que tomamos decisiones estratégicas sobre qué herramienta usar. Para la pregunta de los viajes de ida y vuelta en 10 horas, ¿escogerías una tabla de valores, un plano de coordenadas o una ecuación? Defiende tu elección.
sentenceStemsEs: Otra herramienta que podría funcionar es ___ .

extending.stem: Math is in YOUR world. Describe a real situation from your life that works like the tram problem — a total split into equal groups, or a time built from equal chunks — and show the math.
extending.modelAnswer: My bus ride to school takes 22.5 minutes each way, so one round trip is 45 minutes. In a 5-day school week I spend 45 × 5 = 225 minutes on the bus — that is 225 ÷ 60 = 3.75 hours, almost four hours a week, which I never realized until I did the math.
extending.stemEs: Las matemáticas están en TU mundo. Describe una situación real de tu vida que funcione como el problema del tranvía — un total repartido en grupos iguales, o un tiempo formado por partes iguales — y muestra las matemáticas.

workedExample.work: Apply — What Time Is It? The new year starts at midnight on January 1st. What time will it be 2,022 minutes after midnight?
workedExample.workEs: Aplica — ¿Qué hora es? El año nuevo empieza a la medianoche del 1 de enero. ¿Qué hora será 2,022 minutos después de la medianoche?

workedExample.label: A classmate at our table answered
workedExample.labelEs: Un compañero de nuestra mesa respondió

extending.correctWork: The correct answer is 9:42 a.m. on January 2. 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 remainder 42, so 2,022 minutes is 33 hours 42 minutes. That is 24 hours (one full day) plus 9 hours 42 minutes — 9:42 a.m. on January 2.
extending.correctWorkEs: La respuesta correcta es 9:42 a. m. del 2 de enero. 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 con residuo 42, así que 2,022 minutos son 33 horas y 42 minutos. Eso es 24 horas (un día completo) más 9 horas y 42 minutos — 9:42 a. m. del 2 de enero.
hints: Divide 2,022 by 60 to get hours and leftover minutes.
hintsEs: Divide 2,022 entre 60 para obtener horas y minutos sobrantes.

practice.commonMistake: Converting minutes to hours by moving the decimal point — 625 minutes is NOT 6.25 hours. An hour is 60 minutes, so divide by 60: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42 hours.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Which statement best shows what this lesson means by "math is in my world"?
choices: We visualize real problems, use tools to show relationships among quantities, and choose our tools strategically
Real-world problems can only be solved with a calculator
Tables and diagrams are decorations we add after solving
Every problem must be solved with the same one tool
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes three claims. We visualize and represent problems. We use tools to show relationships among quantities. We make strategic decisions about which tool to use.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has three parts: visualize, use tools, choose strategically.
Which option keeps all three?

turnAndTalk.question: The aerial tram must move 4,000 passengers, and each ride carries 80 passengers. What operation tells you how many rides are needed, and why?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Moving 4,000 passengers in rides of 80 each requires dividing 4,000 by 80.

stems.en: I would ___ 4,000 by 80 to find the number of rides.
stems.es: Yo ___ 4,000 entre 80 para hallar el número de viajes.

turnAndTalk.extend: If each ride instead carried 100 passengers, would you need more or fewer rides than before? Justify without doing the full calculation.
extendStems: With 100 passengers per ride, I would need ___ rides because ___.
This makes sense because larger groups mean ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted 'find how many rides are needed for 4,000 passengers' under division and 'find the total minutes for 50 rides at 12.5 minutes each' under multiplication. What tells you which operation a tram task needs?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Some tram tasks split a total into equal groups (division), while others combine equal groups into a total (multiplication).

stems.en: This task needs ___ because we are ___.
I can tell by looking for ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Explain to a partner how a tape diagram could show one of the division tasks from the board.
extendStems: My tape diagram would show ___ split into ___ equal parts.
This helps because I can see ___.

turnAndTalk.question: One tram round trip takes 35 minutes. Before you can find how many round trips fit in 10 hours, what units problem do you have to solve first?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 10 hours must be converted to 600 minutes before it can be divided into 35-minute round trips.

stems.es: Necesito convertir ___ horas en ___ para que las unidades coincidan.

stems.en: The two quantities in the problem are ___ and ___.
stems.es: Las dos cantidades en el problema son ___ y ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How many round trips fit in 10 hours, and how many minutes are left over? Justify using your table or calculation.

I know this is reasonable because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, one problem asked how many minutes 10 rides of 12.5 minutes each take. What strategy did you use?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 10 rides of 12.5 minutes each is 12.5 × 10 = 125 minutes, since multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place left.

stems.en: I multiplied ___ by ___ to get 125 minutes.
I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who wrote 1.25 minutes instead of 125 minutes? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Their mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

questions.stem: You multiply a whole number by a fraction smaller than 1. The answer is:
choices: Smaller than the number you started with
Bigger than the number you started with
questions.explanation: Taking part of an amount leaves you with less than the whole amount.

parallelPractice.stem: One tram trip takes 12.5 minutes. Build the table: 1 trip → 12.5 min, 10 trips → ___, and use it to find the minutes for 20 trips.

steps.prompt: 10 trips: 12.5 × 10 = ___ (multiplying by 10 shifts the decimal point).
steps.promptEs: 10 viajes: 12.5 × 10 = ___ (multiplicar por 10 corre el punto decimal).

steps.prompt: 20 trips is double that: 125 × 2 = ___.
steps.promptEs: 20 viajes es el doble: 125 × 2 = ___.

hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
